analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.50, indexes it to inflation, and covers farmworkers and home care aides.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $10.50 was never considered: it sat in committee without a single hearing, markup, or vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The Catching Up To 1968 Act would have raised the federal minimum wage to $10.50 an hour and then adjusted it every year to keep pace with inflation, so Congress would never have to raise it again for it to hold its value. It would also raise the cash wage for tipped workers to 70% of the full minimum, extend minimum wage and overtime protections to farmworkers and to home care workers who look after elderly and disabled people at home, and require the Labor Department to announce each increase 60 days in advance. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be the roughly tens of millions of workers paid near the federal minimum: fast-food and retail employees, and especially tipped workers, whose federal cash wage has been frozen at $2.13 an hour since 1991. Farmworkers, who federal law has exempted from minimum wage guarantees, and home care aides, who provide companionship services to elderly and disabled people, would gain coverage for the first time. Indexing to the Consumer Price Index would mean the wage keeps its value automatically, so the lowest-paid workers would stop losing ground to inflation between congressional raises.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage, tipped, farm, and home care workers

how_it_helps.text: It raises the federal minimum wage to $10.50 an hour and then adjusts it each year to keep pace with inflation, so the wage floor stops eroding between acts of Congress.
It sets the tipped minimum wage at 70% of the full minimum, a direct raise for servers and other tipped workers whose federal cash wage has been $2.13 since 1991.
It removes the agricultural exemption so farmworkers — who are currently not guaranteed the minimum wage — would be covered by federal wage and hour law.
It removes the exemption for home care companionship workers, extending minimum wage and overtime protections to home health aides.
It requires the Labor Department to publish each scheduled increase 60 days in advance, giving workers and employers notice of coming changes.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall mainly on employers who pay low wages — restaurants and food service (the biggest users of the tipped minimum), farms, retail chains, and home care agencies — through higher payroll costs. Because the tipped wage would rise sharply, restaurants would bear a disproportionate share. Some of the cost would pass to consumers through prices, and some employers might cut hours or staffing.

drawbacks.text: Raising the federal minimum wage 60 days after enactment would be a fast increase for small businesses with thin margins, particularly in low-cost regions where $10.50 exceeds local prevailing wages.

The bill offered no small-business phase-in schedule or tax offsets; the wage floor would rise on a fixed timetable, and employers with limited ability to absorb the cost would have had to raise prices, cut hours, or reduce staff.

Eliminating the agricultural exemption entirely would have extended overtime and recordkeeping requirements to seasonal farm labor contractors with little administrative capacity, a compliance burden some advocates of the change acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and broad: a higher, inflation-proof wage floor for tens of millions of workers, with explicit raises for tipped, farm, and home-care workers who federal law has long shortchanged. The strongest good-faith objection is that a rapid jump to $10.50 could raise labor costs for small businesses and, in some low-wage regions, cost some jobs or hours — though indexing was designed to soften future shocks. The bill's transparency provisions (advance notice of increases) were a genuine attempt to ease the transition for employers. On balance, the gains to low-wage workers substantially outweighed the acknowledged adjustment costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 21, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 23, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — a step deeper into committee, not a step toward the floor.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the last recorded action is the April 2013 subcommittee referral.
The bill drew 19 cosponsors, all Democrats, none of whom could move it out of committee in a chamber where the committee agenda was controlled by the majority party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying near the federal minimum — restaurants, farms, retail chains, and home care agencies — avoided the wage increase entirely. Their workers, who the bill was written for, got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 23, 2013 and took no further recorded action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee agenda and the floor calendar, and brought no minimum wage increase to a vote during the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 supporters (the sponsor and 19 cosponsors) were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the majority-party committee never acted on it.

industries.note: A higher base wage and a substantially higher tipped minimum directly raise the largest labor cost line for restaurants, which employ the bulk of tipped workers. Consumers would see some of this passed through in menu prices.

The bill eliminates the farmworker exemption, so farm operations would for the first time owe the federal minimum wage and overtime to nearly all employees. Farm labor is low-paid, so the cost impact is concentrated.

industries.industry: Home care and home health agencies
industries.note: Removing the companionship-services exemption means home care agencies and families employing aides directly would owe minimum wage and overtime. This raises costs for agencies but ends sub-minimum pay for a nearly all-female, low-wage workforce.
Any employer paying near the federal minimum would face higher payroll costs. For workers, the same change is the entire point of the bill.
